anchor: Come to me in the silence
title: Echo: title and date
short: Written in 1854 and published in Goblin Market (1862); the title points to the nymph Echo, wasting away for a lost love.
body: Rossetti composed the poem in 1854 and included it in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862). In Ovid, Echo is a nymph who can only repeat others' last words; rejected by Narcissus, she pines until only her voice remains. The title thus suggests a voice repeating a past love, and a woman who has faded into memory. The poem itself is an invocation, repeated 'Come', to the beloved who survives only in dreams.

title: speaking silence
short: An oxymoron: dreams are silent yet speak; the phrase also fits Echo, a voice with no body.
body: The 'speaking silence' of a dream is the poem's central paradox: the dead or lost beloved can speak only in the silence of sleep. Repetition of 'Come' (anaphora) in the first lines gives the effect of a voice calling into emptiness, perhaps answered only by echo. The beloved comes 'with soft rounded cheeks and eyes as bright / As sunlight on a stream', the youthful face preserved in memory.

title: memory, hope, love of finished years
short: The speaker addresses not only the beloved but the memory, hope and love of years now ended.
body: The line is ambiguous: 'of finished years' may govern all three nouns (the memory, hope and love belonging to a past that is over). 'Finished' means ended, but may also suggest perfected or complete. Biographers have linked Rossetti's poems of lost love to her broken engagement to the painter James Collinson (ended 1850), though such readings are speculative and the poem may equally lament someone dead.

title: 'too bitter sweet'
short: The dream is too sweet because so bitter on waking: the paradox goes back to Sappho's 'bittersweet' Eros.
body: Sappho called love 'glukupikron', sweet-bitter (fragment 130), and the idea of love's sweet bitterness became a commonplace of Petrarchan poetry. Rossetti's escalation, 'how sweet, too sweet, too bitter sweet', makes the dream's sweetness the cause of pain. The dream's 'wakening should have been in Paradise': that is, it ought to have ended not in ordinary waking but in heaven, where 'souls brimfull of love abide and meet'.

sources.cite: Christina Rossetti, The Complete Poems, text by R. W. Crump, notes and introduction by Betty S. Flowers (Penguin Classics, 2001), notes

title: Paradise
short: Rossetti imagines a Paradise where loving souls 'abide and meet'; the dream promises a reunion the waking world denies.
body: For a devout Anglican like Rossetti, reunion in heaven was a real hope, and many of her poems wait for it. 'Paradise' in Christian usage can mean the place of the blessed dead awaiting resurrection (Luke 23:43, 'To day shalt thou be with me in paradise'). 'Brimfull' (brim-full) suggests souls filled to the edge with love. The stanza contrasts the souls who 'meet' there with the 'thirsting longing eyes' that watch the door, which are also in Paradise, longing for those who have not yet arrived.

sources.cite: Christina Rossetti, The Complete Poems, text by R. W. Crump, notes and introduction by Betty S. Flowers (Penguin Classics, 2001), notes

title: the slow door
short: The door of Paradise opens to admit souls but 'lets out no more': the dead cannot return.
body: The 'slow door' is the gate of Paradise or of death, watched by 'thirsting longing eyes', which by the syntax belong to souls already within Paradise, waiting for those still outside. 'That opening, letting in, lets out no more' is a compressed line whose present participles mimic the slow swing of the door. The image recalls the parable of the wise and foolish virgins, 'and the door was shut' (Matthew 25:10). The irrevocability of the door explains why the speaker must rely on dreams.

sources.cite: Christina Rossetti, The Complete Poems, text by R. W. Crump, notes and introduction by Betty S. Flowers (Penguin Classics, 2001), notes

title: 'that I may live / My very life again though cold in death'
short: The speaker asks to relive her real life in dreams, though she herself is 'cold in death' while waking.
body: The syntax is ambiguous: 'though cold in death' may refer to the beloved, who is dead, or to the speaker, whose waking life is a kind of death. Either way the poem inverts life and dream: only dreaming is 'my very life'. 'Pulse for pulse, breath for breath' imagines a reciprocal, bodily exchange, recalling biblical formulas of exact exchange ('eye for eye', Exodus 21:24) transformed into love.

title: 'Speak low, lean low': the close
short: The final couplet slows to short, repeated phrases, ending on 'how long ago!' like a fading echo.
body: The poem has three six-line stanzas rhyming ababcc, with iambic pentameter lines and shortened fourth and fifth lines (a trimeter, then a dimeter: 'Come back in tears', 'Watch the slow door', 'Speak low, lean low'). The final line, 'As long ago, my love, how long ago!', repeats 'long ago' as an echo would, fulfilling the title. The beloved is asked to whisper and bend close, as in life, but the repeated phrase stresses the distance in time.

title: stanza form and refrain
short: Each stanza's short fifth line is a turning point, contracting the verse before the closing pentameter.
body: The pattern of three pentameters, a trimeter, a dimeter and a final pentameter gives each stanza the shape of a breath drawn in and released. 'Come back in tears' asks the beloved to return weeping, perhaps as tears of reunion or as the speaker's own tears that bring the memory. The repeated verbs 'come', 'come back' structure the poem as a single prolonged appeal.
